title: "Aesthetics is for LOSERS" (A Defense of Anime & Bodybuilding)
summary: Response to Alec Enkiri's video mocking anime fans who chase aesthetics. NH argues that fans copy the physique because anime powers are impossible, that shonen is about self-improvement, that aesthetics matter as much as function in both fiction and real life, and that functional-training contempt for bodybuilding comes from resentment.
claims: Anime fans copy their heroes' physiques rather than their feats because the feats (flying, energy blasts) are impossible; you take the part that is reachable
The real goal of shonen is not physical superiority or getting jacked but self-improvement; strength and physique are only means to that end
There is no bad motivation to start training: if the reason leads to self-betterment it is the right reason, including wanting an anime character's physique
Male power fantasies (Greek heroes, anime) deliberately combine impressive physique and feats to inspire young men; form and function complete each other
Dragon Ball Super got worse because power-ups stopped being shown by the body getting bigger; removing the aesthetic side breaks the power fantasy
Humans are primarily visual: people judge others first by looks, so a big person is assumed strong regardless of actual lifts
In real life looking strong is effectively being strong, since nobody can see how much you bench; aesthetics are what matter socially
Bodybuilders brag about being weak to mock people who think lifting more plates earns respect in daily life
Natural bodybuilding in the broad sense (anyone lifting to look better) is by far the most popular fitness pursuit online; ~90% of fitness media is bodybuilding in disguise
Pro bodybuilding is a fringe sport; people confuse it with natural bodybuilding, which is the pursuit of health and human perfection
CrossFit only became popular once its athletes looked jacked (with PEDs); before that it was mocked
Olympic weightlifting and MMA gained mainstream attention mainly because their athletes look muscular, not for the function itself
Powerlifting boomed around 2010 because people distrusted PED-fuelled bodybuilding and sought another way to get jacked; those viewers later left when it did not deliver aesthetics
Calisthenics would not be popular without the aesthetic reward of a V-taper and six-pack
People who claim to train only for function usually want abs and shoulders deep down; chasing aesthetics as a byproduct of a sport you do not love leads to disappointment
There is no such thing as a non-functional muscle; a developed muscle functions
You cannot reach aesthetics without developing function; bodybuilders simply evaluate function by what it does for the look
Maxing out function hurts form and vice versa: you cannot be both an elite sprinter and an elite bodybuilder; most should prioritize one and get some of the other
Being heavy and muscular makes him slower and less athletic; basketball players should not take his advice, but he can still walk and hike for hours
Being able to lift heavy does not make you a better fighter
Bodybuilding is an aristocratic, artistic practice of sculpting the body, while strength sports descend from an era when function was needed for survival
Self-improvement requires honesty with yourself: if aesthetics will make you happy, embrace them and ignore those who call it bad
